From depth to time

How a phone video became a spatial object in Blender. First the video was turned into depth and built as a point cloud. Then the frames were stacked into a volume of time and cut with a slice. The last version uses a red colour clip, Comp 2.

Environment
Blender 5.2 LTS, Geometry Nodes, Time Block 0.2.2
Footage
iPhone clips IMG_4324, IMG_2952; Comp 2.mov
Processing
Video Depth Anything, FFprobe, FFmpeg
Final version
Comp 2, 0 to 20 s, 600 frames

Fig. 1 Process and scope

The scope moved from making a video play inside space to making time itself a material.

01Capture

Short walking clips shot on iPhone: a hallway (IMG_4324, 5.7 s) and a metal slide (IMG_2952). A moving camera gives the depth model parallax to work with.

02Process the video into depth

Each clip goes through Video Depth Anything, which estimates depth for every frame and writes a greyscale video. White is near, black is far. The output keeps the original framing, so colour and depth line up pixel by pixel.

03Exploration A: depth point cloud

A 9:16 plane is scattered with 50 000 points. The depth video pushes each point along Z, and the colour video paints it. Both movie textures read the scene frame, so the cloud plays with the timeline.

Solid lines carry geometry; dashed lines carry texture data. File: Depth Map924 / Depth Map926.blend.

What it showed: the scene reads as real space, but only one moment is ever visible. Time is still playback. This led to the second method.

04Method study B: time as an axis

With the Time Block add-on, every frame becomes a flat X·Y plane and the frames stack along Z. Z now means time. A slice cuts through the stack; what it shows depends on where it cuts and at what angle.

Every frame is one X·Y plane; the frames stack along Z.

Scope grew in three tests

Before building, FFprobe reads the clip and FFmpeg extracts frames into a PNG cache page (an atlas). The shader reads every slice from this page. Each test made the clip longer.

05Final: the red version

Comp 2 (1280 × 720, 30 fps, SDR) built as a time volume: 600 samples, shown as a stack of 122 semi-transparent planes, with one large slice through it.

In Blender

Reading the volume: what each cut shows

These cuts are taken from the same 600 cached frames the slice shader reads.

Settings of the final version

SettingValueWhat it does
Source range0 to 20 s at 30 FPS600 samples from a 60 s clip
Cache320 × 180 px tiles, 14 × 43 gridOne PNG page, about 20 MB
Volumeheight 2.82, time depth 11.86, time scale 1.08Size of the block; Z length = time
Stack122 planes, scale 0.62, depth scale 0.82, opacity 0.84A see-through sample of the frames
Sliceopacity 0.54, emission 4.54The brightest layer, so the cut reads first
Time position0.96Where the slice sits in time (0 = start, 1 = end)
HiddenFront video, multi-sliceKept off so the slice is the only cut

Fig. 2 Comparison

A Depth point cloudB Time Block
InputColour video and a depth videoOne SDR video
GeometryPoints scattered on a planeFrame planes and cutting slices
Z axis meansDepth in the sceneTime
Time appears asPlayback, one frame at a timeA spatial axis you can cut
Motion comes fromThe timelineMoving the slice
StrengthReads as a real scene with volumeShows motion as form, slit-scan images
LimitNeeds a depth estimate; time is never seen at onceNo scene depth; planes only

Fig. 3 System diagram

The piece sits between the cached frames and the camera: one time volume, one slice, one time position.
